synb-01-c1.text: iGEM Foundation (2023). Celebrating 20 years of standard biological parts. iGEM Blog.
synb-01-c1.quote: In 2003, Tom Knight published an assembly method for standard biological parts
synb-01-c1.claim: Knight's 2003 manifesto proposed BioBricks, DNA fragments

synb-01-c3.text: MIT Technology Review (2007). A Safe and Simple Arsenic Detector. MIT Technology Review.
synb-01-c3.quote: A student team from the University of Edinburgh has genetically engineered bacteria to detect arsenic in water.
synb-01-c3.claim: the Edinburgh 2006 arsenic biosensor (color-changing E. coli detecting arsenic in water)

synb-03-c3.text: T S Gardner, C R Cantor, J J Collins (2000). Construction of a genetic toggle switch in Escherichia coli. Nature.
synb-03-c3.quote: The toggle is constructed from any two repressible promoters arranged in a mutually inhibitory network.
synb-03-c3.claim: Gardner, Cantor, and Collins built a toggle switch: two repressors (LacI and a temperature-sensitive λ cI) each repressing the other's promoter.

synb-02-c2.text: Daniel G Gibson, Lei Young, Ray-Yuan Chuang, J Craig Venter, Clyde A Hutchison 3rd, Hamilton O Smith (2009). Enzymatic assembly of DNA molecules up to several hundred kilobases. Nature methods.
synb-02-c2.quote: We describe an isothermal, single-reaction method for assembling multiple overlapping DNA molecules by the concerted action of a 5' exonuclease, a DNA polymerase and a DNA ligase.
synb-02-c2.claim: Gibson assembly, published by Daniel Gibson at the J. Craig Venter Institute in 2009, lets you join multiple DNA fragments in a single isothermal reaction at 50 °C.

synb-07-c1.text: Daniel G Gibson, John I Glass, Carole Lartigue, et al., J Craig Venter (2010). Creation of a bacterial cell controlled by a chemically synthesized genome. Science (New York, N.Y.).
synb-07-c1.quote: We report the design, synthesis, and assembly of the 1.08-mega-base pair Mycoplasma mycoides JCVI-syn1.0 genome starting from digitized genome sequence information and its transplantation into a M. capricolum recipient cell
synb-07-c1.claim: a chemically synthesized 1.08-Mb copy of Mycoplasma mycoides transplanted into a recipient M. capricolum cell, which then booted up controlled by the synthetic chromosome

synb-08-c1.text: Denis A Malyshev, Kirandeep Dhami, Thomas Lavergne, Tingjian Chen, Nan Dai, Jeremy M Foster, Ivan R Corrêa Jr, Floyd E Romesberg (2014). A semi-synthetic organism with an expanded genetic alphabet. Nature.
synb-08-c1.quote: the first organism to propagate stably an expanded genetic alphabet
synb-08-c1.claim: In 2014, Romesberg showed an engineered E. coli could stably replicate plasmid DNA containing a single dNaM-d5SICS pair, given a nucleotide transporter from a microalga to import the unnatural triphosphates.

synb-05-c1.text: C J Paddon, P J Westfall, D J Pitera, et al (2013). High-level semi-synthetic production of the potent antimalarial artemisinin. Nature.
synb-05-c1.quote: fermentation titres of 25 grams per litre of artemisinic acid
synb-05-c1.claim: achieved industrial yields of ~25 g/L by 2013

synb-08-c3.text: Vitor B Pinheiro, Alexander I Taylor, Christopher Cozens, et al., Philipp Holliger (2012). Synthetic genetic polymers capable of heredity and evolution. Science (New York, N.Y.).
synb-08-c3.quote: With the use of polymerase evolution and design, we show that genetic information can be stored in and recovered from six alternative genetic polymers based on simple nucleic acid architectures not found in nature
synb-08-c3.claim: Philipp Holliger's MRC-LMB group, in a landmark 2012 Science paper, evolved polymerases that replicate XNA from DNA templates and reverse-transcribe XNA back to DNA.
